title: Master Blaster: the Dave Marsh Experience
author: Jeffrey St. Clair
content:
[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/marshstonepony.png)](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/08/28/master-
blaster-the-dave-marsh-experience/)

[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/marshstonepony.png)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LJhzS0lY84w)

Dave Marsh at the Stony Pony club in Asbury Park, extolling the virtues of
Southside Johnny and the Asbury Jukes. (Screen capture from video posted to
[YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LJhzS0lY84w).)

> They like to get you in a compromising position  
>  They like to get you there and smile in your face  
>  They think they're so cute when they got you in that condition  
>  Well I think it's a total disgrace
>
> I fight authority, Authority always wins  
>  I fight authority, Authority always wins  
>  I’ve been doing it since I was a young kid  
>  I come out grinnin'  
>  I fight authority, Authority always wins
>
> – John Mellencamp, [The Authority
> Song](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wsEwK69LXjQ)

Writing is fighting, Ishmael Reed said, and to know the writer Dave Marsh was
to fight with Dave Marsh. To have been friends with Dave Marsh was to fight
even more fiercely with Dave Marsh. Most of these disputes were trivial to the
outsider, but vital to the combatants, such as: who was the supreme bluesman,
Howlin' Wolf or Muddy Waters.

A typical conversation I dug out of an old email file…

> Marsh: Wolf didn't even have a competent guitarist.
>
> JSC: He had Hubert Sumlin. Marsh: Sumlin couldn't even play lead. Me: He had
> Willie Johnson, who invented the power chord.
>
> Marsh: He did not. And even if he did, power chords aren't lead.
>
> JSC: He had Jody Williams.
>
> Marsh: Well, I like Jody Williams.

These disputes could linger and ferment for years. The longer they went on,
the deeper in his trench Dave tended to burrow. I admired him for that. It was
a sign of his loyalty—a loyalty to Muddy Waters and to his own view of Muddy
Waters.

In going back over nearly two decades of emails and journal entries, our
debates often sounded less like a Marvin Hagler vs. Ray Leonard bout than
Abbott versus Costello. More often than not, they involved baseball,
eventually.

> Marsh: What are you listening to?
>
> JSC: The Kinks.
>
> Marsh: Why them?
>
> JSC: Why not?
>
> Marsh: They're too fey.
>
> JSC: Define "too fey."
>
> Marsh: Anything fey is too fey.
>
> JSC: Even Fay Vincent?
>
> Marsh: Especially [Fay Vincent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fay_Vincent).

And on it would go, circles in the round, as Miles Davis might say.

Of course, that fit Dave's reputation: irascible, contentious, querulous, and
there's certainly truth to the caricature. But Dave Marsh couldn’t be
pigeonholed. He wasn't just a pugilistic critic. He was a man in full, as Tom
Wolfe said. Maybe a man overfull. He was certainly overflowing with ideas,
passions and biases, but also with curiosity, compassion and empathy. If you
were Dave's friend, you were entitled to fight with him, but it also meant
that he would come to your defense, even when few others would. He came to
mine several times: after gratuitously hostile reviews of books, after
threatened libel actions, after being smeared as Putin’s fool on the front
page of the _Washington Post,_ a paper I used to write for on occasion!

Yes, Dave was a battler. But he saved most of his ammo for the bigger fights,
real ones, not just squabbles, against real enemies who Dave wanted to recruit
you into battle against: the death penalty, the cancer merchants, apartheid
and Sun City, war mongers and war profiteers, Tipper Gore and the music
censors, union-busting corporations and racist cops, Ticketmaster and the
larcenous nature of the music industry, which ripped off artists and fans
alike. The intramural verbal sparring was a kind of training session for the
larger, more consequential battles that united us.

Our friend Daniel Wolff once said, and likely said more than once, that he
chafed at being referred to as a “music writer.” I know what he means and I
feel the same way about Marsh. Yes, nearly all of Dave’s books, of which there
are several shelves worth, take music as their jumping-off point. But what he
was really writing about was life in America. He was a writer whose
interests–political, aesthetic and economic–extended far beyond clickbait-like
disputes over what bands were better, the Dead or Bruce Springsteen and the E
Street Band, The Who or The Clash. He wanted to explore what artists like
Springsteen and the Dead said about the culture that produced them and the
fans who embraced or rejected them and why. Music for Marsh was a gateway to
writing about American culture in the age of neoliberalism: its systemic
racism, its social and economic inequalities, its prisons and cop-haunted
streets, its war-making machines and, perhaps most vitally, how people,
especially America’s youth cultures, were fighting to take control of their
own future and throw off the shackles that circumscribed their lives, even as
the odds were stacked heavily, even lethally, against them.

+++

I've been reading Dave Marsh since I was 12, an awkward kid in Indianapolis
who liked baseball, comic books, horror movies and rock music. Not necessarily
in that order. My grandmother managed a small drugstore on the city’s
southside. She didn't deal Big Pharma’s products, but she sold everything else
in the store, from candy to condoms to magazines. Each week she'd grab a few
comics, like _MAD_ and _Tomb of Dracula_ , for me to read on Saturday nights.
One week her haul included a copy of CREEM, sandwiched between a volume of
_Creepy_ and _Vampirella._ She probably thought CREEM was a horror magazine.
She probably wasn't wrong. After all, they published Lester Bangs.

They also published Dave Marsh. As the Detroit writer Michael Jackman told me,
"To grow up in a Detroit where you could drop out of Wayne State University,
walk down the street, and start writing for Creem magazine." Not only write
for it, but edit it.

Marsh wrote about music the way I talked about music or wanted to talk about
music, when I could find someone who liked or even heard of the MC5 or Iggy
Pop and the Stooges or The Who. Mostly the kids I knew listened to country or
slop rock, like Rush, Journey or REO. Marsh didn't write in fancy prose. His
sentences were raw and unadorned. It got right to the point. His reviews and
essays were pared down, direct, stiletto-sharp and driven home with a
vengeance. Which isn't to say that he didn't have style. But the style was
like the music or paintings or films that he favored, shorn of pretense and
artifice and filler.

When I first started writing about music at age 15 for microscopically small
local rags in Indy, some of them printed on pages of mimeographed paper
stapled together, handed out usually for free at record stores and head shops,
I tried to write like Dave Marsh and quickly proved that imitation isn’t
necessarily the sincerest form of flattery, especially when the writing of the
imitator is crap, which mine surely was. Most of the pieces had Marsh’s
punkish attitude (in excess), but lacked the knowledge and skill for how to
deploy it.

A few years ago, a friend sent me a copy of a story I’d written on Bob Seger,
based on an interview I’d somehow managed to worm my way into before Seger and
the Silver Bullet Band’s gig on the same bill with Queen at the Convention
Center in Indianapolis, one of the nation’s worst concert venues, whose
acoustics resembled the Ford Rogue River engine plant. The interview lasted
about three minutes max, but I turned it into a rambling 3,000-word piece
filled with gratuitous insults and snide asides about an artist and band that
I really enjoyed. I was trying to be tough, but it came out sounding almost
puerile in its conceit.

I told Marsh about it and read him a few of the more overblown passages. He
laughed. How many thousands of kids had tried to mimic his style and fallen on
their faces? The style was one thing, the mind behind it another entirely.
“You know there was a lot more to Seger than you might think.” This from the
man who trashed Seger’s _Against the Wind_ album in a review which led to
punches being thrown and even landing, depending on which account you believed
or wanted to believe.

But Seger was from Detroit. Of course, there was more to him.

“You had to know how Seger started to understand how far he’d fallen,” Marsh
said. “After all, he did write one of the best anti-war songs.” I nodded like
I knew what the hell he was talking about. That was news to me. But a few days
later a CD of early Seger arrived in the mail, containing the song Dave was
referring to: “2+2,” which also rocked harder than almost anything else Seger
recorded.

I probably saw Seger six or seven times. He never performed it. Apparently,
he’d left those sentiments far behind. But Dave hadn’t. War was always on his
mind, largely because America hadn’t stopped making them and people hadn’t
stopped dying or being maimed in them.

“Didn’t you write about Queen?” Marsh asked.

“No, I couldn’t listen to them.”

“Then you missed the story, St. Clair”

No, shit. Again?

But Dave had already gotten the story on Queen. He had dubbed them “the first
truly fascist rock band.” Marsh was a one-man Antifa strike force of record
reviewers. Consider this acidic takedown of Queen's _Jazz_ album:

> The guiding principle of these arrogant brats seems to be that anything
> Freddie & Company want, Freddie & Company get. What's most disconcerting
> about their arrogance is that it's so unfounded: Led Zeppelin may be as
> ruthless as medieval aristocrats, but at least Jimmy Page has an original
> electronic approach that earns his band some of its elitist notions. The
> only thing Queen does better than anyone else is express contempt……..
> Whatever its claims, Queen isn't here just to entertain. This group has come
> to make it clear exactly who is superior and who is inferior. Its anthem,
> "We Will Rock You," is a marching order: you will not rock us, we will rock
> you. Indeed, Queen may be the first truly fascist rock band. The whole thing
> makes me wonder why anyone would indulge these creeps and their polluting
> ideas.

Over the top? Maybe. But the invective is delicious to read. It’s why I
started calling him the [Master
Blaster](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rJtxiE5pbR0), after Stevie Wonder’s
tribute to Bob Marley and the role music played in the black liberation
movements of post-colonial Africa and the Caribbean.

I have multiple copies of the [_Heart of Rock and
Soul_](https://www.hachettebookgroup.com/titles/david-marsh/the-heart-of-rock-
soul/9780306809019/) and the first two editions of the [_Rolling Stone Records
Guide_](https://archive.org/details/rollingstonereco00mars) because I have
consulted them so obsessively over the years that the spines cracked and the
pages are falling out. They also tend to disappear, as in being swiped. I
found a lost copy of both, along with Dave’s rollicking book on “[Louie
Louie](https://press.umich.edu/Books/L/Louie-Louie),” on Cockburn’s shelves
down on the Lost Coast, a couple of months after he’d set up shop in our house
for a week. “Oh, yes, meant to return those, Jeffrey. Tell Marsh good stuff.
Very good stuff.” First the “borrowing,” then the praise. Both high
compliments from the Master.

Dave's writing seemed immediate even when he was writing about the past,
especially when compared to some of the other notable rock critics of his era,
Christgau, Marcus and Guralnick, whose prose often seems moribund even when
writing about the present, as if the music they were writing about were a
corpse on the table awaiting their dissection. Check out one of his last
books, a slim volume on [The Beatles’ Second
Album](https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/594212/the-beatles-second-
album-by-dave-marsh/), where he made music we’d all heard hundreds of times
sound fresh, vibrant and capable of speaking to our own turbulent moment.

The rankings don’t mean much to me anymore. Marsh’s taste was idiosyncratic
and often contrary to the point of insolence. But his acerbic and concise
assessments of the music meant everything, rivaled as artifacts of late-
capitalist cultural criticism only by David Thomson’s _Biographical Dictionary
of Film._

And that’s not to say Marsh couldn’t get it wrong, sometimes spectacularly so,
as in his critical assessment of Neil Young, who in one of the longest and
most zig-zagging reviews in the [_New Rolling Stone Record
Guide_](https://archive.org/details/newrollingstoner00mars), he dismissed as
“a minor artist.” I suspect Dave’s “mind-made body” will be wandering a few
extra years in the Bardo to purge that misjudgment.

**+++**

[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/marshrecordreview.png)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=a-R4q3ERTzo)

Marsh rating records from the window of the CREEM offices. (Screen capture
from video posted to [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=a-R4q3ERTzo).)

In a not-so-simple twist of fate, two decades after I’d churned out my
juvenile imitations of Dave Marsh, Dave Marsh was writing for me at
_CounterPunch_. In fact, three of my favorite writers as an adolescent (a
developmental stage I rigidly clung to until about the age of 30) ended up
writing for publications I edited: Cockburn, Marsh and Ishmael Reed. The day
Ishmael Reed’s first submission to _CounterPunch_ landed in my inbox, I was
more excited than Steve Martin’s character in [_The
Jerk_](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-7aIf1YnbbU) when he found his name in
the phone book. I went running down the hall, waving a printout of his piece,
yelling, “A story from Ishmael Reed, _the_ Ishmael Reed!!” Fortunately, only
the cat and the dog were around to observe this sorry spectacle. I felt much
the same way when Marsh’s first story for us hit my email box.

As you might expect, Dave’s copy was usually pretty clean, certainly cleaner
than Cockburn’s, especially when Alex was submitting typewritten pieces by fax
with ink-smudged hand-scrawled corrections. Still, Marsh’s submissions weren’t
immaculate. Yet like many editors, Dave took light–and I’ll emphasize
“light”–edits graciously or at least sedately.

Of course, turnabout was fair play and once Dave entered the _CounterPunch_
stable of writers, he didn’t hesitate to offer his own editorial advice on my
pieces. I recall being sternly admonished for using the word “transgression”
in a sentence.

> Marsh: It’s pretentious.
>
> JSC: It’s part of the common language.
>
> Marsh: It’s French.
>
> JSC: It’s Latin. Trans means “to step.” Gress means “over.” To step over.
>
> Marsh: You proved my point. Why get complicated and Latinated? Just write
> “cross” or “violate” or “trespass.”
>
> JSC: Trespass sounds kind of French, Dave.
>
> Marsh: Touché.

In his pieces for us, Marsh attacked Clear Channel for banning “questionable
music.” He denounced the “orgiastic [![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/kick-out-the-
jams-9781982197179_xlg.jpg)](https://www.simonandschuster.com/books/Kick-Out-
the-Jams/Dave-Marsh/9781982197179)patriotism” of “God Bless America.” He
skewered the “vigilantism” of the RIAA and its collusion with the FBI. He
wrote a heart-wrenching plea to save the life of death row inmate Byron
Parker. He mocked the music industry’s inane and self-defeating war on
cassette tapes. He ridiculed Jann Wenner’s decision to hire editors at Rolling
Stone who believed that “people didn’t have time to read.” He exposed the
hypocrisy, thievery and “stupid folklorist purism” of the widely (and
absurdly) venerated Alan Lomax. He recalled hearing a 10-year-old boy sing all
of the lyrics to Springsteen’s “41 Shots” (about the police killing of Amadou
Diallo), writing, “Kids learn songs like ’41 Shots’ only at home. That song
got played a lot by people who know that it could also be their kid lying on
the cement.” He heaped righteous abuse on Bono, as the useful tool (and fool)
of the global elites, dubbing him the “mascot of neoliberalism.”

Dave wrote more than [75
essays](https://www.counterpunch.org/author/bar4waja/) for _CounterPunch_
before veering off forever into that diabetes of the mind called podcasting. I
say this as a writer and a reader. I say it as someone who loved hearing Dave,
and his cohost on _Live From the Land of Hope and Dreams_ , Kevin Alexander
Gray, talk. But I preferred their writing. Their books and essays are
something I can, and do, go back to again and again. Podcasts are ephemeral;
writing endures (so far). Its meaning deepens over time. Both of their lives
were cut too short and I miss what they could have put down on the page. As it
is, the last piece Dave wrote for us was published on May, 3, 2016. It was a
prescient warning about the false allure of the Bernie Sanders campaign that
served as something of a template for the themes and tone of my own book on
Sanders published later that year.

The meaty, beaty and bounciest of Dave’s essays were collected by his pal
Daniel Wolff into _[Kick Out the Jams: Jibes, Barbs, Tributes and Rallying
Cries from 35 Years of Music
Writing](https://www.simonandschuster.com/books/Kick-Out-the-Jams/Dave-
Marsh/9781982197179)._

+++

We hit it off, at first, for reasons having (almost) nothing to do with music.
We were both from the industrial Midwest. We both loved dogs and baseball. We
liked many of the same writers, especially Ross MacDonald and Dashiell
Hammett. We both despised the Clintons and Clintonism. The fractures, such as
they were, came later, even on these mutualities, like active fault lines on
shared terrain.

The fireworks between us didn’t flare up until 1997 or 98 when we started the
CP email list for _CounterPunch_ writers and friends. It had some heavy
hitters, few heavier than Dave, though when it came to debating something,
anything really. We posted new stories, editorials, interviews, celebrity
gossip, jokes, drafts of stories and generally gave each other’s writing a
good-natured slagging. Cockburn once described it as like “an editorial
meeting of the _New Left Review,_ but for people who had a sense of humor and
knew what the hell they were talking about.” I’m not sure about that
assessment, but it was lively and free-ranging and usually fun, with Marsh
often the center of the action, ripping Bono’s “execrable doggerel” and Al
Gore’s “monosyllabic mush.”

Marsh was a world-class name-dropper, a veritable B-52 of dropping names,
which often served as the knock-out blow in many arguments, especially with
me. But then Dave knew a lot of names. And I mean “knew” them, not just how to
spell them. Even so, he was an incredibly generous person. Generous with his
time, generous with his knowledge and generous with money. And not generous in
the way Hemingway described Scott Fitzgerald, as “always being willing to lend
a helping hand to the person a step above him on the ladder.” Dave was
generous to people who needed help: people who were sick, people in prison,
struggling writers, new bands, old blues players without health care, young
rappers whose music had been banned or stigmatized with warning labels.

I recall when CP-lister Christine Karatnytsky, a librarian at the NYPL for the
Performing Arts, challenged Dave’s dismissal of Pink Floyd as self-indulgent
and aimless art rock, Dave responded by asking her to write a piece for _Rock
and Rap Confidential_ defending the merits of the band. There was a chivalrous
side to him even when he was mixing it up. With men, he would often leave no
quarter.

Marsh used to say that the people on the _CounterPunch_ email list were too
polite. He told me he belonged to an "F List," which required all of the
members to use "fuck" at least once in each post. I guess that's how he got
his juices flowing in the mornings. He didn’t really need my help, though I
enjoyed kickstarting anyway, because once he got started it was like hearing
Bob Dylan go electric; the sparks would fly and you never knew what he was
about to burn to the ground.

+++

Marsh and I didn’t meet in the flesh until the summer of 2000 when I came to
New York City to promote the release of _Al Gore: a Users’ Manual_ , a book
which Dave had been an essential resource for, especially in our scathing
account of Tipper Gore’s career as a moral prude and music censor.

We had lunch at a Spanish place on the Upper East Side and afterwards walked
to the Frick Museum, perhaps the most significant contribution to American
culture ever made by a union-busting robber-baron. My eyes tended to glaze
over at the Renaissance paintings of Madonnas Dave found so fascinating (no
Diebenkorns or DeKoonings in this stately beaux-arts mansion), but they
finally lit up when we encountered the museum’s three small Vermeers, which,
of course, Dave had informed notions about.

Then the conversation took a sudden swerve from Vermeer to Verlaine. Marsh was
fully capable of Davesplaining about both. Not quite sure which Verlaine Dave
was going on about, Paul or Tom, I diverted him towards Dylan’s fascination
with the former (“[You’re Gonna Make Me Lonesome When You
Go](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Claf8E18eLs)”) because being back in NYC
for the first time in decades, where I’d heard Television play so many times
in college, I wasn’t in the mood to hear him ridicule Tom for tuning his
guitar like Jerry Garcia or some shit. (Any comparison to the Dead, no matter
how tangential, meant Marsh was about to consign a band to Hell and I don't
mean [Richard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Hell).)

According to my notebook, the conversation unfolded something like this…

> JSC: So, you’re not a big fan of _Blood on the Tracks_?
>
> Marsh: You’ve heard the original [New York
> takes](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fL6MCURttck&list=PLhf15HNg3QRUPvia5ujtZHq_6dqP_4Tc2),
> right?
>
> JSC: No.
>
> Marsh: Of course, you haven’t.
>
> JSC: I haven’t heard everything, Dave. I was only 15 and on a lawn-mower’s
> budget when Blood on the Tracks came out. Plus, I hadn’t had that much
> heartbreak in my life yet to relate to it.
>
> Marsh: You haven’t heard it because Dylan didn’t _want_ you to hear it. He’s
> the absolute worst judge of his own material. The New York band’s better,
> more electric and energetic than the amateurs he recorded the official
> release with in Minneapolis. But you can see his obsession with arcane
> symbolism creeping in that would metastisize full-blown esotericism in
> _Street Legal._ And why’d he leave “Blind Willie McTell” off _Infidels?_ Who
> the fuck knows.

We went our ways. I was scheduled to give a talk that night with Cockburn at
the Judson Memorial Church on Washington Square in the Village. But instead of
thinking about what I was going to say, I spent the remainder of the afternoon
going from one record joint to another (back when NYC had record joints)
trying, unsuccessfully, to track down bootlegs of the electric version of
“Blind Willie McTell” and the New York sessions of _Blood on Tracks_.

When I got back to Oregon a week later, there was a parcel stuffed with CDs
that Marsh had burned containing all of those tracks, along with the [Complete
Basement
Tapes](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PL26aYop7IFXe36w3ziZecbEVH2E03_QMV).
He also included a bootleg of The Who’s scuttled
[Lifehouse](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ge2Vyxq7S1Q) project, which he
assumed, correctly as usual, I hadn’t heard either. After our exchange in NYC,
Dave had apparently concluded that my knowledge of music was deficient. He
wasn’t wrong.

The beginning of my music education, courtesy of Dave Marsh, came through the
mail. Once or twice a month, in boxes of CDs posted from Norwalk, Connecticut,
arrived in Oregon City containing Delta blues, Chicago blues, R&B, doo-wop,
bluegrass, 50s rock, soul, gospel, hip hop, you name it. It was Marsh’s
version of the Columbia Record Club. Over the next few years, He turned me on
to artists, contemporary and historic, I'd missed or prematurely dismissed:
[Charley Patton](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=336dDZsU1Eg), [Magic
Sam](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-OlA_JVbQl8), [Clarence
Carter](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tj8eAHn_2YM), [Clifton
Chenier](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pE35yfOn6cg&list=PLOFsCPXqLYfpjct80OM6iUWB_77h7EOMG),
[Gatemouth Brown](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mXLO1HL0SoQ), [Slim
Harpo](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-5x7NIqga8M), [the Five
Royales](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tKR_lzci83I), [the Blind Boys of
Mississippi](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2BjErw_B1FQ), [Dorothy Love
Coates](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DfFaPZndgvo), [The
Kingsmen](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CfRZNNyQoF0) (naturally), [Bobby
"Blue" Bland](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FRa9-66QcoA), [Otis
Rush](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aa7NKOor-Sk), [Charles Wright & the
Watts 103rd Street Rhythm
Band](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=F-MQQPlUPEE&list=RDF-
MQQPlUPEE&start_radio=1), [Ray Wylie
Hubbard](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ygTsN_sr4k8), [Rodney
Crowell](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1rOJ31bioeY), [Patty
Griffin](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pOI5E1MdqGU), [Chris
Buhalis](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=d3_MrjLugo8), [Iris
Dement](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nlaoR5m4L80), [Otis
Taylor](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=I7FROFtNNfY), [Robert Bradley's
Blackwater Surprise](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KHWZ_MMnuX0), and
[Stewart Francke](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gPTdzGsn_0U). All of whom
continue to be in heavy rotation on my playlists. Many of whom I couldn’t get
through a week without hearing.

+++

Dave’s profound sense of loyalty and solidarity derived from the blue-collar
workers and union members of his Motown milieu and the factories of Flint,
Pontiac and Dearborn. He was a veteran of many pickets, in spirit if not
always in body, and he loathed scabs. He was a fan of music and sports, but he
understood these endeavors were industries not different in kind from the auto
industry of his hometown and just as exploitative. When he wrote about his
beloved Tigers or the Chicago blues, he examined the political economy of
these enterprises, but thankfully not in the opaque language of the economist.
He wrote with the verve and clarity of a shop steward.

In the late-90s, I remember Marsh being peeved at Jackson Browne, an artist we
both admired for his music and political activism. (Marsh wrote the incisive
liner notes for [The Very Best of Jackson
Browne](https://www.rhino.com/product/the-very-best-of-jackson-browne) album.)
Marsh griped that Jackson spent too much time “on international” issues and
not enough on “our various domestic crises.” I thought this was a pretty
strained argument coming from one of the leaders of the [Artists Against Sun
City](https://archive.org/details/suncitybyartists00mars) (South Africa)
campaign, especially given the fact that US-trained death squads were still
rampaging freely across Central America and US corporations treated all of the
western hemisphere as their private fiefdom for human and environmental
exploitation. Was Jackson’s disgust at this appalling state of affairs truly
an international fixation? I don’t know how firmly Marsh actually believed
this proto-America First! stance, but once he dug into his trench, it would
take either mustard gas or someone bombarding him with the “[Piña Colada
Song](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TazHNpt6OTo)” to drive him out. You have
to admire that kind of stubbornness, up to a point.

This too, though, could be written down to his sense of loyalty, sticking
doggedly to an editorial position that _Rock and Rap Confidential_ had staked
out in defense of a kind of class-based American economic populism that it
found and celebrated in the music of Bruce Springsteen and John Mellencamp. In
fact, Cockburn once asked after reading one particularly “homegrown” issue of
RRC, “Do Marsh and (co-editor Lee) Ballinger really think John Mellencamp is
going to lead the Revolution?” I was on shaky ground here. For seven years,
Mellencamp had lived just down a few gravel roads from us in southern Indiana
and I knew several of his band members. In fact, the toddler version of
Nathaniel St. Clair refused to have his locks shampooed by anyone other than
Mellencamp’s hairstylist, who lived in the forested hollow behind us on a
former commune 15 miles from Bloomington. “Well, he makes more sense than
Howard Dean, doesn’t he?”

Cockburn could scarcely argue the merits of that point.

**+++**

Dave Marsh had a restless mind that ranged across a vast spectrum of subjects:
the paintings of Arthur Dove, the cinema of John Ford, the novels of James M.
Cain and Andrew Vachss, the intricacies of major league baseball’s collective
bargaining agreement. He read voraciously: trade papers, memoirs, economics,
cancer research, the congressional record, trial transcripts, the Baseball
Abstract, unsolicited manuscripts, poems, performance riders, FBI files. You
name it. He was a polymath, though he would have hated the word. Too Latin. Or
too Greek, maybe. Certainly, too fey.

Dave and I talked about writing a book together, a dual biography of the two
Willie Hortons, the slugger for the Detroit Tigers World Series champions and
the Massachusetts man whose criminal history was exploited in racist attacks
against Michael Dukakis, first by Al Gore, then by George HW Bush. The project
never came to fruition. I wrote it off as being “too French” in concept.

After that crazy idea fell through, I told him I wanted to investigate the
murder of the legendary Stax drummer Al Jackson, Jr. He warned me off. He said
he knew enough about the case to realize “the real story still couldn’t be
told.” Dave seemed to know where the trail led. But he wasn't about to lead me
there. “Dangerous places and dangerous people,” he said.

On the night of October 1, 1975, Al Jackson, Jr., the genius keeping time for
one of the greatest rhythm sections in American music history, was shot and
killed inside his home in Memphis. Stax Records died a few months later. Was
there a connection? Jackson had a troubled domestic life. Two months before he
was killed, his wife Barbara had shot him in the chest as the marriage was
spiraling towards divorce. Jackson refused to press charges. The Memphis cops
wrote it off as a case of self-defense. On the night of his murder, Jackson
was returning home late from a boxing match when he was shot in the back five
times. Police found him next to his estranged wife, Barbara, who was on the
floor, her hands tied behind her. She told the police an intruder had forced
his way into the house and restrained her, as he attempted to rob the house
until Jackson arrived.

But there were many unanswered questions, uncomfortable questions about the
killer and the cops. It looked more like a hit than a robbery. Nothing was
taken from the house, which contained a stash of cash and jewelry. Jackson’s
wife had ties to a local gang leader. The cops didn’t look very hard. Some say
they were intimidated or, more likely, just didn’t care about the killing of
another black man, even one as prominent as Jackson. No one was charged or
even arrested and the case remains unsolved.

I ignored Marsh’s warnings and began to follow some of the sinister threads of
the story, one of which led improbably to Seattle, where the darkness of the
story didn’t end at the edge of town, but spread all the way down. But after
six months, I hit a series of dead ends (fortunately I wasn’t one of them) and
couldn’t pin down my suspicions about the hidden hands behind Jackson’s murder
with any certainty and filed it away.

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/Phil_Spector_mugshot.jpg)

In this police booking photo released by the Los Angeles County Sheriff's
Dept. showing Rock music producer Phil Spector after he was convicted Monday
April 13, 2009, of second-degree murder in the shooting death of actress Lana
Clarkson at his mansion in 2003. (AP Photo/Los Angeles County Sherriff's
Department)

A few years, after abandoning the Al Jackson project, I got a call from the
celebrated music producer and gun fanatic Phil Spector, who was then under
investigation for the murder of Lana Clarkson, a struggling actress who
moonlighted at the House of Blues, where Spector picked her up one night and
drove back with her in a limousine to his castle-like compound in the LA
suburb of Alhambra.

There was an icy, menacing quality to Spector’s voice. I asked how he’d gotten
my number. “Dave Marsh gave it to me. He said you might be able to help me
out. The cops have got it all fucking wrong. I didn’t kill that woman. She
offed herself, man.” I’m not easily spooked, but I found his whole rap
unnerving. After Spector hung up, I rang Marsh.

> JSC: “What the fuck, Dave?”
>
> Marsh: “What the fuck what?”
>
> JSC: “You told Phil Spector to call me?”
>
> Marsh: “Sure.”
>
> JSC: “You said I’d tell his story?”
>
> Marsh: “No. I said you’d _investigate_ his story. You’re a journalist,
> aren’t you? You write about police abuse all the time, don’t you?” He was
> right. I didn’t know how trustworthy Phil Spector was (not very, I
> suspected), but I knew no one should trust the LAPD. So, I talked to Spector
> a few more times. He told me his unlikely version of what happened that
> night, which was that Clarkson was drunk and depressed and while she was
> handling one of Spector’s guns (he owned dozens), she shot herself in the
> mouth. It was a case, Spector claimed, of “accidental suicide.” But under
> the rules set out by Spector’s legal team, I couldn’t quote Spector. It was
> clear that he wanted me to write what he told me as if it were a scenario
> I’d verified. Well, that wasn’t going to happen.

Still, I looked into Clarkson’s life. I read the police and coroner reports
and, years later, the defense assessment from OJ Simpson’s hired forensic gun,
Dr. Henry Lee. I checked the backgrounds of the lead LAPD detectives in the
case. Spector’s version of events didn’t hold up to scrutiny. But I felt
better about myself for running it down. Dave was right. I should have
welcomed the call, not been prematurely creeped out by it.

Around this time, I started writing about death penalty cases and discovered
that Dave had gotten there. He was a fierce opponent of state-sanctioned
killing. He knew death penalty lawyers and prisoner support groups. He knew
members of Congress who opposed the death penalty and clergy who ministered to
death row inmates. He knew how to arrange death row visits and gave keen
advice on how to talk with inmates and their families. Since then, I’ve
covered nearly 25 death penalty cases, and I've quoted what he said to me very
early on: "It doesn't take any moral spine to oppose the execution of an
innocent person. The real test is opposing the execution of people you know
are guilty. I don't want the state killing someone in my name and you
shouldn't either."

+++

[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/marshwolff.png)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vpJWP1Jo70Q)

Marsh and Daniel Wolff at the Woody Guthrie Folk Festival 2017. (Screen
capture from video posted to
[YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vpJWP1Jo70Q).)

Dave endured the cruelest of fates, being locked in a functioning body as his
awesome mind faded, dissipating day by day from a degenerative brain disease
that for the last few years of his life left him unable to read, write and
ultimately communicate or think. Dave Marsh had vanished long before his body
finally gave out.

Marsh left us with questions that maybe only he was positioned to get the
answers to, since he always contended that the closer a writer got to his
subject, the deeper the obligation the writer had to hold them accountable.
And few writers were closer to Bruce Springsteen than Dave Marsh. Shortly
after Springsteen's 9/11 album _The Rising_ came out, Dave called to ask me if
I thought the song "[Empty Sky](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GwpcTn1djC8)"
might have been a reference to Edward Said's book.

I had to tell Dave that he'd gotten the title wrong. Edward's terrific book on
the daily lives of Palestinians under Israeli occupation was called _[After
the Last Sky](https://cup.columbia.edu/book/after-the-last-
sky/9780231114493/). _He was disappointed, a potential essay spoiled. I had
the sense that Dave wanted to see something in Springsteen that was,
inexplicably for him, absent. He wanted Springsteen, the musician he'd
invested so much of journalistic energy in trying to understand and portray on
the page, to feel the same compassion for Palestinians that he did. But he was
searching for things that weren't there. Even today, Springsteen has said
nothing about Gaza, nothing about a genocide unfolding before his eyes. I
would have enjoyed debating Dave about that. It would have pitted Dave's
loyalty to Springsteen against his deep sensitivity for human suffering and
his hatred of mass killing, especially when done with US financial support and
US-supplied weapons.

And once we'd thrashed that out, we could have fought about Bruce's adoption
of [dynamic ticket pricing](https://variety.com/2022/music/news/bruce-
springteen-ticketmaster-ticket-prices-rise-thousands-dynamic-
pricing-1235321657/) for his concerts, a greedy strategy for the troubadour of
working-class America that pushed ticket prices well beyond the reach of most
of his lifelong fans, leaving the audiences at his live performances packed
with private equity types, who were likely making deals on their cellphones to
loot companies and fire workers while Bruce played the “Ghost of Tom Joad.”

+++

Dave Marsh was the first friend to call the morning after Alexander Cockburn
died. He said he knew how hard it was going to be to keep _CounterPunch_ going
in the wake of Alex’s death and the kind of burden that was suddenly going to
fall on my shoulders to do all of the story recruitment and editing for both
the print newsletter and the website. He warned I’d be tempted to stop writing
and just edit and fundraise, but in reality I needed to pick up the pace and
write for two. (Not the fucking advice I wanted to hear. I was already putting
in 65 to 70 hours a week.)

“You’re not Cockburn,” he said. “But then he wasn’t you.” He’d been through
tumultuous transitions at _CREEM_ , _Rolling Stone_ and the _Village Voice_.
He pledged to write more frequently, help with the editing and send money. He
did all three. “Focus on the writing and the editing,” he urged. “The money
will come and if it doesn’t, then fuck them. They don’t know what they’ll be
losing.”

The money came in trickles and freshets. Even a few substantial checks from
notable musicians landed in the Post Office at the General Store in Petrolia,
perhaps at Dave’s prodding. Our stable of writers grew as well. There
developed what I called the Marsh Circle (AKA, the Flintstones): [Lee
Ballinger](https://www.counterpunch.org/author/qlussuw111/?__cf_chl_tk=h3ta09tWLn8Ja3hkMPklk0mwkv2uFe_DjUYkzTJHkY8-1787796953-1.0.1.1-zA.9AYi6ZdcL6fOzhAEoUj.43_H18Pc0hAYklL6T8J0),
Susan Martinez, [Bill
Glahn](https://www.counterpunch.org/author/chuwuf5mexechuw/), [Kevin Alexander
Gray](https://www.counterpunch.org/author/fegu2ehe/), [Phyllis
Pollack](https://www.counterpunch.org/author/b2ebugaqacru8eh/), [Daniel
Wolff](https://www.counterpunch.org/author/draphe/), [Steve
Perry](https://www.counterpunch.org/author/psxacxd111/), [Harry
Browne](https://www.counterpunch.org/author/spiath/), [Michael
Donnelly](https://www.counterpunch.org/author/michael-donnelly/), [John
Sinclair](https://www.counterpunch.org/author/s6ahemabufesabu/). We survived.
Turned the corner and hit the gas.

Then a few months after Alex died, our daughter was diagnosed with a rare
lymphoma. And Dave Marsh was one of my own first calls. His daughter Kristen
had died of cancer, a mercilessly aggressive sarcoma. For two years, Dave went
through every brutal step of the illness and treatment with her. He devoted
himself to understanding the disease, its origins and treatments; its costs,
financial and emotional. Dave wrote a short guidebook to cancer. In some of
his clearest prose, he demystified a disease that so many people were still
too scared to talk about.

No one expects their kid to get cancer. No one expects them to face the
possibility of death before 30. But Dave’s book advised us how to ask the
right questions of doctors and nurses. It gave us ideas for how to deal with
the incessant demands of hospital administrators and insurance companies.
Dave’s book was a tremendous comfort at a perilous moment in our lives. It
gave us this sense that we could get through this and we did. I’ve shared it
with many others facing similar diagnoses in the years since.

But Dave helped even more. He didn’t just email his book, send good wishes and
vanish into the ether as many would have and, in fact, some friends did. He
either phoned or emailed every day through the 30 days of radiation therapy
and the weeks of follow-up treatments. He was there to talk through the nausea
and lack of sleep, the tedium and anxiety, the economic and work pressures,
the fear that even when being beaten into remission it might come back. Dave
was there to help us stay grounded and keep us from spiraling into paranoia
and despair. We weren’t special. Dave made a similar effort with countless
others. (See Holly Gleason’s terrifically tender, funny and intensely moving
account in her essay “[Dave Marsh
Calling.”)](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/08/24/dave-marsh-calling/)

Marsh knew all of this because he forced himself to learn the hard facts. Most
people’s initial reaction to a potentially fatal diagnosis in a loved one is
to turn away from the diagnosis and the future it portends. That was certainly
mine. But Dave understood that cancer was just a disease. Cancer isn’t just
pain and fear and anguish. Cancer’s also a business. It’s a business often as
ruthless as the disease itself that can and often does bankrupt families
regardless of the success of the treatment. It’s why he fought so hard to make
health care a basic human right, at least as sacrosanct in the American
conscience as owning a gun, and to strip the profit motive out of treating
people with life-threatening illnesses. That’s the kind of fighter (or even
just [hand to hold on to](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0LyUCy3eOvs)) that
you want by your side when you find yourself under punches.

In the end, Dave Marsh’s assessment of Warren Zevon could well be said about
Marsh’s own writing and way of living: “Smart enough to teach, quick enough to
learn, dedicated enough to hold both ends together.”

You kicked the fuck out of the jams, Dave.
